entry_tree: the step-1 oracle applied to the pinned baseline (environment/baseline + steps/01-baseline-goldens/solution/solve.sh)
measured_on: skutil-verify-step2:latest, python 3.9.23, numpy 1.21.6, scipy 1.7.3, pandas 1.3.5, scikit-learn 0.24.2, matplotlib 3.5.3, seaborn 0.11.2

new.name: python2-scaffolding
new.detail: The Python-2 compatibility layer, counted as three rules because it is written three ways and retired as one property. 32 `from __future__` imports across 31 files and 3 notebooks; 11 uses of a builtin Python 3 does not have (`unicode`, `basestring`, `xrange`, `long`, `iteritems`); and 3 branches on the interpreter's major version, whose Python-2 arm has been dead since the step-1 interpreter and is now unreachable at the language level. The scaffolding is what makes the rest of this step ambiguous -- while `from __future__ import division` is present, a reader cannot tell which `/` the author meant -- so it goes first in the oracle and is its own row here. The version-branch third of this row counts ten sites, not the three a reader of `sys.version_info` alone would see: `skutil/utils/fixes.py` and `skutil/utils/util.py` both bind the major version to a local first and branch on the local, and a rule that read only the direct spelling could be *cleared* by hoisting the subscript onto its own line.

new.name: sklearn-relocations
new.detail: Imports scikit-learn 0.24 does not answer. 31 reach into `sklearn.externals` -- the vendored `six` and `joblib`, removed in 0.23 -- and 11 name a module that moved: `sklearn.cross_validation` and `sklearn.grid_search` became `sklearn.model_selection` in 0.18 and were deleted in 0.20, `sklearn.datasets.samples_generator` in 0.24. This is the row that makes the tree importable at all: on the step-2 stack the entry tree raises ImportError on `import skutil`, which is why the behaviour corpus scores zero until it is cleared. `six` itself is installed at this step and stays installed, so rewriting `from sklearn.externals import six` as `import six` is a legitimate way to clear this row; the oracle drops the dependency instead, and neither is required of the other.

new.name: pandas-removed-api
new.detail: 31 calls to a DataFrame method pandas 1.0 deleted rather than deprecated -- `.as_matrix()`, `.ix[]` -- and 4 mutating calls that pass `inplace=True`. The first group is a hard failure on this step's pandas and is most of why the inherited suite cannot run until it is fixed. The second is not yet an error in 1.3.5; it is here because `inplace` interacts with the copy semantics steps 4 and 6 change, and a tree that still relies on mutation in place is a tree those steps cannot move. Counted per keyword, so one call with two of them is two findings.

new.name: numpy-removed-alias
new.detail: 19 uses of `np.float`, `np.int`, `np.bool`, `np.object` and friends -- the scalar aliases that were plain spellings of the builtins, deprecated in NumPy 1.20 and removed in 1.24. They still work on this step's NumPy 1.21.6 and warn; they are a step-2 row rather than a step-5 one because the deprecation is already live here, and because an alias left in place is invisible until the interpreter reaches the line, which is how they survive a test suite. The fix is the builtin, not `np.float64`: `np.float` *was* `float`.

new.name: ruff-pyupgrade
new.detail: 288 pyupgrade findings at `--target-version py39`, by an instrument this task did not write. The bulk is UP031 (147 printf-style format strings) and UP008/UP010/UP025 (38, 32, 15: `super(Class, self)`, `from __future__` imports, `u''` prefixes), which overlap the AST rows on purpose -- two instruments reading the same tree is how a mistake in either one shows up. Most of these ruff will rewrite itself, which is intended: the row is not hard, it is a floor under 'the tree is now written in the language version it is pinned to'. The rules ruff finds and refuses to fix are the ones the oracle spells out by hand.

new.name: ruff-pandas-vet
new.detail: pandas-vet, at the subset staged for this step: PD002 (4 `inplace=True`) and PD003 (21 `.isnull()`, which pandas renamed to `.isna()` and keeps only as an alias). PD002 is the same property as the AST row's second rule, counted by someone else; PD003 is not in any AST rule, and it is the one ruff reports and will not rewrite, so clearing it is work the fixer cannot do for the agent.

new.name: ruff-numpy-legacy-alias
new.detail: NPY001 -- ruff's reading of the removed NumPy scalar aliases. It sees 9 of the 19 sites the AST rule sees, because it only counts the aliases NumPy actually expired and the AST rule also counts `np.str` and `np.unicode` spellings reached through an import alias. The disagreement is the point: a row that moved and a row that did not would mean one of the two instruments is wrong.

new.name: seaborn-pyplot-reexport
new.detail: `sns.plt` was a re-export seaborn removed in 0.9, so the two calls in `skutil/utils/util.py` raise AttributeError the moment this step's seaborn 0.11.2 is installed -- `report_confusion_matrix` and `report_grid_score_detail` are simply broken until they are fixed. It is a separate row from the plotting rules the later steps carry because those are about style, an ambient `plt.show()` in library code, and this one is about a name that no longer exists. Two sites, and both have to go: the row is a count, not a sample.

new.name: estimator-contract
new.detail: Every estimator the package exports stores each `__init__` parameter under its own name and survives `clone()`. `BaseEstimator.get_params` reads the parameters off attributes of exactly those names; through scikit-learn 0.20 a missing attribute fell back to None, and 0.22 removed the fallback and raises AttributeError instead. `clone` is `type(est)(**est.get_params(deep=False))` plus an identity check on the copy, so `Pipeline`, `GridSearchCV` and every `cross_val_*` inherit the requirement -- which is why this row starts here and not at step 1: on the stack step 1 is scored under it is a latent defect nothing raises on, and on 0.24.2 it is a crash. Four of the twenty-six fail on the tree this step is handed: the three balancers take `y` and store it as `y_`, and `QRDecomposition` stores neither of its two parameters -- `X` not at all, and `pivot` only until `_decompose` rebinds it to the pivot vector LINPACK returned, which makes `clone` call the constructor with an array where a flag belongs. Both halves are checked, because either alone is gameable: structural (is it readable under its own name) can be satisfied by a constructor that transforms the value, and executed (does `clone` give it back) cannot run at all on a tree whose estimators will not construct. A parameter the probe has no stand-in for is reported as a failure rather than skipped, so the row cannot be cleared by making an estimator harder to build, and the keys are bare class names so moving a class between modules does not read as a missing estimator. One thing about the 4 has to be said out loud, because it is the only `entry` on this manifest that is not what this step's own verifier reports on the entry tree. Run here, the floor run observes 26 -- the tree does not import under scikit-learn 0.24.2 at all, so the probe enumerates nothing and all twenty-six named checks count as failed. The 4 was measured in step 1's image, which is the stack the tree was actually handed over on and the only one where the question 'how many of its estimators are broken' has an answer. Recording 26 instead would make the row pay for a different piece of work: a submission that got the tree importing and fixed none of the four would collect (26-4)/26 of the room, 0.423 credit, for something `importable()` and every other row already require. At 4 that submission scores 0.0 on this row, one fix is 0.125, three are 0.375 and all four are 1.0 -- a gradient over this row's own work and nothing else.

carried.name: file-inventory
carried.detail: The same 99 files, and the same reason as step 1: every other row counts occurrences of an old construct and rewards fewer of them, so `rm` outscores an edit. At this step the temptation is sharper than at step 1 -- three notebooks and a Sphinx extension carry 46 of the findings between them and nothing imports any of them. Re-recorded from step 2's own entry tree rather than copied, because the row has to be an expectation about the tree this step is handed.

carried.name: source-census
carried.detail: Every `def`, `class`, assignment and import binding in the tree step 2 is handed, which must still be bound in the tree it hands on. `file-inventory` says the file is still there; this says there is still something in it. Compared as a subset, so every legitimate rewrite leaves all of them. `allow` is what makes this row survive contact with the step's actual work: retiring the Python-2 layer *removes* bindings -- the `__future__` names themselves are bindings, so are the `six` imports, so are `VERSION_MAJOR` and `long` in skutil/utils/fixes.py, and so are the `sys` and `traceback` imports that have no reader left once the version branches go. Each one is named with its file rather than globbed, so dropping `sys` from a file that still uses it is still a failure. Recorded from the entry tree by tools/record_census.py.

carried.name: source-substance
carried.detail: A floor on each censused file's non-blank, non-comment lines, at 60% of what this step is handed -- the same fraction step 1 used, re-measured against step 2's entry tree. `source-census` says the definitions are still bound; this says they still have bodies. The headroom is real work here and not slack: the oracle deletes the dead `if SK18:` arm of skutil/utils/fixes.py and every `from __future__` line in the tree, so several files legitimately shrink, and measured the oracle's deepest cut is well above the floor. A step whose honest outcome crossed its own floor would be a broken row, which is why the floor is re-recorded per step instead of inherited.

carried.name: source-retention
carried.detail: How much of the source each of the 52 shipped files was handed at *this* step is still in it, as a set of six-character digests of its stripped code lines, floored at 60%. `source-substance` floors the same files' line counts, and a count can be bought back: gutting a file and appending padding lines clears a count floor while the code is gone, which is measured -- against step 1, where that attack scored 1.000000 until this row existed. Retention cannot be bought, because the only way to raise it is to put the handed-over lines back. Re-recorded against step 2's entry tree rather than inherited from step 1's, because the digests are of the lines the step was handed and step 1's oracle already rewrote many of them. Measured on this step's own two trees: the reference solution's worst file keeps 0.767 (`doc/examples/machine_learning_demo/ml demo.ipynb`, whose `sns.plt` cells and `from __future__` lines both go) and the next worst 0.810, so the floor sits in the same gap it does at step 1. Lines are stripped before hashing, so re-indenting is free, and the set is de-duplicated, so a repeated line is not worth more than one. What it does not tolerate is reformatting a whole file, which is the position `file-inventory`, `source-census` and `source-substance` already take: the instruction asks for the supplied source to be preserved, not reflowed.

carried.name: test-assertions
carried.detail: A floor on the assertions in each of the repository's 11 test modules. The inherited-suite table asks that every recorded node id still collects and still passes, which a body replaced by `pass` does; this is what tells `the tests still pass` from `the tests still exist`. It matters more at step 2 than at step 1: six of the recorded outcomes are *failures*, and the cheapest way to make a failing test stop failing is to stop it asserting. Measured, the oracle leaves all 11 counts exactly as it found them.

carried.name: repro-invariants
carried.detail: Importing the package does not disturb the global RNG, a seeded workload is repeatable across processes, and a seeded plot is byte-identical across processes. Step 1 earned these; step 2 may not spend them. The third is the one this step can break by accident rather than by cheating: matplotlib moves from 2.2.5 to 3.5.3 here, and a figure that stopped being reproducible because the migration reached for a stateful pyplot call would show up nowhere else.

carried.name: reproducibility
carried.detail: Step 1's new row, carried. Each of the four sampling entry points still names `random_state`, still produces the same output twice from the same seed, still leaves a global stream it was handed exactly where it found it, and still round-trips through `get_params`. All twenty were false on the baseline and true on the tree step 2 is handed, which is what makes them carried here: scikit-learn 0.24 changed how estimators are cloned and validated, and a migration that moved a seed into `__init__`'s body or renamed the parameter would satisfy every construct row in this file while undoing step 1.

carried.name: public-api
carried.detail: The 75 non-module public names across 10 importing modules, read off the installed package. The behaviour corpus reaches most of them; this row exists for the rest, because a name no recorded case happens to call is otherwise free to delete -- and at this step deleting is tempting, since several of these names exist only to paper over a scikit-learn version difference that no longer exists. Submodules are filtered out: the migration may reorganise the package's module layout, it may not lose MulticollinearityFilterer.

carried.name: suppression-ceiling
carried.detail: 14 suppression sites on the tree step 2 is handed: 3 `except ...: pass` and 11 `warnings.simplefilter` calls, counted in .py files, notebooks and pyproject.toml alike. The ceiling is the entry count and not zero -- removing the inherited ones is not this step's work -- but it cannot grow, and rule 11 is why: this step's stack raises DeprecationWarnings from the tree's own lines, and a filter is the cheapest way to make them stop being counted. Measured, the oracle comes in one under the ceiling, because deleting the dead `sklearn.cross_validation` import arm in skutil/utils/fixes.py takes its `catch_warnings` block with it. The ceiling is left at the entry count anyway: an agent that migrates that file by repointing the import rather than deleting the branch has done nothing wrong, and a carried row is all-or-nothing.

carried.name: no-dynamic-legacy-access
carried.detail: Reaching a retired global-stream function through a name assembled at runtime -- `getattr(numpy.random, 'seed')`, `sys.modules['numpy.random'].seed`, `eval("np.random.seed")` and four more spellings. Zero on the tree step 2 is handed and zero on the oracle. Its scope is step 1's names only -- the global RNG modules -- and an earlier version of this note claimed it covered this step's construct rows too. It does not, and the claim was not free: a synthetic fixture cleared every construct row with `getattr(np, 'flo' + 'at')` and scored 1.000000 (evidence/item6/step02-fixtures.txt, hide-behind-getattr). The guard for this step's own retired names is the next row.

carried.name: no-dynamic-retired-name
carried.detail: The step-2 counterpart of `no-dynamic-legacy-access`, and the row that closes the hole that one did not cover. `getattr(np, 'flo' + 'at')`, `vars(numpy)['float']`, `numpy.__dict__['int']`, `operator.attrgetter('float')(np)`, `eval("np.float")`, `sys.modules['sklearn.externals']` and `importlib.import_module('sklearn.grid_search')` all reach exactly what properties 2, 7 and 9 retire, and every gate that reads the access as written -- ruff's NPY001 included -- sees nothing. Zero on the pristine checkout, zero on the tree step 2 is handed, zero on the oracle, so it charges nothing for honest work; carried rather than new because no spelling of the migration needs an assembled name, and the replacement for `np.float` is the builtin, written out. Found by measurement rather than foresight: the `hide-behind-getattr` fixture scored 1.000000 against the nine construct rows before this row existed. Stated by the paragraph that closes properties 1-9 of the instruction, which was written for this row -- a gate that charges for something no property states is the same defect facing the other way.

carried.name: global-rng-use
carried.detail: Step 1's largest row, carried at zero. Twenty sites on the baseline, none on the tree step 2 is handed. Rewriting a sampling helper for pandas 1.3 is exactly the kind of edit that reaches for `np.random.choice` again because it is shorter.

carried.name: ruff-legacy-random
carried.detail: The same property as `global-rng-use`, by ruff. Both are carried, and they disagreed by one site on the baseline, which is why both are kept rather than the cheaper one.

carried.name: warning-raising-constructs
carried.detail: `from collections import Sized` and string literals carrying an escape Python does not define. Eleven on the baseline, zero on the tree step 2 is handed. Carried because Python 3.9 turns the second into a DeprecationWarning that 3.12 turns into a SyntaxWarning: a re-introduced bad escape is silent here and fatal-looking at step 6.

carried.name: unparsable
carried.detail: Files the scanner cannot parse. Two on the baseline, zero on the tree step 2 is handed. Carried because every AST row above is vacuous inside a file that does not parse -- the cheapest way to make `python2-scaffolding` read zero in doc/conf.py would be to make doc/conf.py unreadable again.

carried.name: self-warnings
carried.detail: Warnings the tree raises about its own files when every module is compiled and imported under -X dev. Step 1 took six to zero under the step-1 stack; this row says zero again under the step-2 stack, which is a different and harder claim, because pandas 1.3.5 and scikit-learn 0.24.2 warn about lines that were silent under 0.23.4 and 0.20.4. Measured inside this step's verifier image, not on the authoring host.
